intended_object: The functor (C ⥤ₗ D) ⥤ (Grp C ⥤ Grp D) that sends a left-exact functor F between cartesian monoidal categories to its induced functor on group objects, F.mapGrp, and sends a natural transformation α to the natural transformation whose component at a group object A is α_A, seen as a group-object morphism. Taken from the docstring ("`mapGrp` is functorial in the left-exact functor").
explanation:
The definition is the one in Mathlib itself, so there is no other Mathlib declaration to cite.

On objects it sends F to F.1.mapGrp. Here F.1 is made monoidal by `Monoidal.ofChosenFiniteProducts`, which works because a left-exact functor preserves finite products.

On morphisms it uses `Grp.homMk''` applied to α.hom.app A.X. This is correct because, between cartesian monoidal categories, a natural transformation between product-preserving functors automatically respects the group structure. So each component α_A is a morphism of group objects F(A) → G(A), and naturality follows. Identity and composition are inherited componentwise. This is exactly the functoriality the docstring describes.

On generality: the construction only needs F to preserve finite products, not all finite limits, so it would still make sense on the category of finite-product-preserving functors. However, Mathlib has no bundled category of product-preserving functors. The docstring explicitly fixes the domain as left-exact functors, and this matches the existing `C ⥤ₗ D` infrastructure. The analogous `mapMonFunctor` for monoids is indexed by lax monoidal functors, which is the natural setting there. I judge restricting the domain to left-exact functors a reasonable design choice, not a clear case of being too narrow.
